title: Describing people
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: sie DOES THREE JOBS and this module opens no row for any of them — L1-M2 owns the key, with its note already true of all three. The separating rule is the VERB: sie ist is "she is" (singular), sie sind is "they are" (plural, lowercase), Sie sind is "you are" (plural, capital in the middle of a sentence). The index cannot see the capital and never will, so the verb is what a reader has to go by.

The possessive "her" is taught on ihre ALONE — feminine and plural: ihre Schwester, ihre Kinder. That is a key nothing else holds, because L1 kept the possessive ihr out so that Ihr Name could own the polite "your". Where a masculine possession is needed, the sentence takes the von periphrasis — der Bruder von Anna — which is ordinary spoken German and not a workaround.

Every adjective in this level stands AFTER sein and takes no ending: Er ist groß, Seine Haare sind kurz, Ihre Augen sind blau. That is a decision rather than an oversight — an adjective in front of a noun has to be declined, and the declension is L3's. So features are stated predicatively and the module never writes ein netter Mann.

das Mädchen is NEUTER despite meaning "girl", and it is the most famous fact about German gender. The reason is mechanical: -chen makes anything neuter, whatever it means. Gender is a property of the WORD and not of the thing, which is what makes it learnable at all.

Frau is L1-M2's key, where it is the title in Frau Weber — and it also means "woman" and "wife". One key, three readings, exactly as sie has three. Mann does the same: a man and a husband, with only the sentence to say which.

words.note: Its plural takes an umlaut and nothing else — Brüder. A capital, because every German noun has one.
Its plural adds -n. The sch is one sound, a sh, and the w after it is a v.
L1 showed ich heiße and mir but never the possessive itself. mein goes with a masculine or neuter noun and meine with a feminine or plural one.

words.note: The possessive "her", lowercase, and it is a different key from L1-M2's capital Ihr. Only the capital tells a reader which is meant, and only for feminine and plural things.
der Bruder von Anna is "Anna's brother", and it is ordinary spoken German rather than a workaround. It takes the dative, which L3 will make visible.
The third-person cell of L1-M1's heißen — that row owns the infinitive, and this is the shape a third person takes. German asks what someone is CALLED, and the ß is a long s.

words.note: mein Freund can mean a boyfriend as well as a friend. ein Freund von mir is the safer way to say the second thing.
The -in ending makes a feminine person out of almost any German job or role, and it doubles the n in the plural.
The final -ig is said -ich in standard German, with the front ch sound. That is regular for every -ig ending.

sentences.usage: Describing someone, and the gender is the point.

words.note: Two readings on one word, exactly as Frau is a woman and a wife. Only the sentence says which, and der Mann von Anna is the second.
Herr adds -n everywhere except as a bare subject — von Herrn Weber, Herrn Weber sehen. A small group of masculine nouns behaves this way.

sentences.trap: German's ordinary way of saying "Herr Weber's wife" is die Frau von Herrn Weber. The -s possessive exists — Herrn Webers Frau — and the von frame is what people say.
